title: Rootpath correlation & request-log debugging walkthrough - Auriga Systems
summary: Redwood product walkthrough focused on Console tracing, request log correlation across services, KV cache fallbacks, and security constraints for a private deployment. Customer wants to validate debug and incident workflows and schedule a pilot with live traces and synthetic load.
action_items: Jules - provision a demo tenant with sample traffic by 2027-10-08
Samir - share SOC2 + network connectivity doc and pricing spreadsheet by 2027-10-06
Liam - provide example anomalous trace IDs and typical traffic profile by 2027-10-07
next_steps: Send security package and network diagram (Samir)
Run 24h synthetic pilot on Dedicated instance (Jules & Auriga)
Follow-up call with Priya to confirm KMS/HSM options and SSO configs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run through the Redwood Console focused on tracing and request forensics. I know Auriga has some tight SLOs so we'll show rootpath correlation and how you can stitch logs and spans across service boundaries.
[00:00:12] Marta Ruiz: Thanks, Samir. Quick context: we run a multi-service inference stack, some on-prem and some cloud, and we see intermittent 5xxs during model switchovers. We need to be able to trace user request through the gateway, router, and model pool.
[00:00:28] Jules Kim: Got it. I'll share my screen and start in the Console. First note - apologies if the transcription gets messy, sometimes the tool swaps a few names.
[00:00:35] Jules Kim: (screen share) This is the Trace Map. Each node represents a service span - HTTP gateway, routing service, the Redwood runtime, and then the model host. We automatically generate a rootpath ID that threads through the request.
[00:00:50] Liam O'Neill: How deterministic is that rootpath ID? Is it from our request header or generated server-side?
[00:00:58] Jules Kim: Good question. We prefer to ingest your existing correlation IDs if present (x-request-id). If not, the runtime will synthesize a rootpath id at ingress and propagate it. You can see here, the trace view shows both types and an inferred mapping when it detects overlapping times and metadata.
[00:01:18] Marta Ruiz: We use x-amzn-trace-id sometimes and a custom request-id. Will Redwood accept multiple correlation headers?
[00:01:26] Jules Kim: Yes. You can configure multiple header names in the ingestion mapping. The Console UI surfaces which header was used as the canonical id.
[00:01:34] [00:01:35] Priya Das: Sorry to jump in — on the security side, how long are these traces kept? Are they stored encrypted with customer keys?
[00:01:44] Samir Patel: Short answer: configurable retention and encryption. For Hosted we have default retention but you can opt into Private with your own KMS keys or Dedicated with customer-managed keys. Jules will show where audit logs and export hooks live.
[00:01:58] Jules Kim: Right. On the left nav, there's an Exports panel. We can push traces to your S3 or GCS, or ship to your SIEM. For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM via the key wrapping APIs.
[00:02:12] Tom Baker: And SSO? We need SAML with role-based access so only SREs can replay traces.
[00:02:19] Rina Alvarez: We've got a SAML connector and RBAC controls. You can map groups to Console roles, and the Request Inspector button can be gated.
[00:02:26] [00:02:30] Jules Kim: Back to the trace - here is an example 5xx. You can click any span to expand metadata: headers, upstream latencies, model variant, token counts, and KV cache hits. See this span flagged as KV-cache-miss with fallback to disk quantized-path - that triggered a spike.
[00:02:48] Liam O'Neill: That timing looks about right. On our side, the pattern is usually a failed cache miss then a burst to cold model which increases latency and sometimes times out. Can you show how we'd find all requests that followed this fallback path?
[00:03:00] Jules Kim: Yep. Use the 'Search by path' filter and pick 'runtime.kv_cache.fallback:true' or similar. You can also build a saved filter that shows correlated logs + traces.
[00:03:10] Marta Ruiz: Are logs auto-stitched or do we need to ship them with the trace id?
[00:03:15] Jules Kim: The Console attempts to stitch logs via matching timestamps and common ids. Best practice is to emit the request id in your logs so stitching is exact. We also accept span IDs for deeper linkages.
[00:03:26] [00:03:30] Samir Patel: I'll call out a feature - Request Playback. Once you find a failed trace you can replay the request against a canary model or a mirrored traffic path. It replays both headers and body and can be run against a dedicated sandbox.
[00:03:44] Priya Das: Replay concerns me from a PII perspective. Does playback redact PII, and how do we ensure it doesn't get routed to a cloud-hosted model if we're in private mode?
[00:03:53] Jules Kim: Playback respects your routing policy. For Private deployments, playback runs inside your VPC. For Hosted, you can opt into a local sandbox or a redaction pipeline; we can also do tokenization callbacks. Redaction is configurable — you can declare fields to mask before saving or exporting.
[00:04:10] Tom Baker: Good. Show me an example end-to-end incident.
[00:04:14] Jules Kim: Sure. Pulling up a real incident (sanitized). This request shows a large increase in model token count at T+120ms after a model variant switch. The trace shows the orchestration service pushed a new model variant, the KV cache invalidated, then ten concurrent requests hit cold-start. You can expand the timeline and see per-span metrics: p50/p95 latency, downstream retry counts, and model response codes.
[00:04:36] [00:04:40] Marta Ruiz: Can we set alerts on those KV invalidations? We want to know before customers see errors.
[00:04:44] Jules Kim: Absolutely. Alerts can be configured on trace patterns or metric thresholds. For example, set an alert if runtime.kv_cache.fallback rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes, and attach recent traces to the alert ticket. We integrate with PagerDuty/Jira/Slack.
[00:04:57] Liam O'Neill: When you attach traces to tickets, is that a link or an export? We have strict controls around data exfiltration.
[00:05:04] Jules Kim: By default it's a link that respects RBAC. You can choose to export a redacted artifact if required. The Console stores audit trails about who viewed or exported traces.
[00:05:16] [00:05:20] Samir Patel: Let's demonstrate a search for high-latency user journeys using tags. I'll pick a user request ID and show session stitching across requests — this is handy when a user session results in progressive degradation.
[00:05:33] Jules Kim: Here we search by user_cookie and time window. The session view stitches several requests. Notice one span shows model_variant: quant-8bit causing token decoding overhead. You can pin that and run a cohort analysis across seven days to see frequency.
[00:05:51] Marta Ruiz: Is cohort analysis run on retained traces or on sampled data?
[00:05:56] Jules Kim: Both. By default we sample heavy traffic but you can enable full retention for certain customers or flows. Cohort analysis on full retention gives precise counts; on sampled data it extrapolates and shows confidence intervals.
[00:06:10] [00:06:15] Tom Baker: Can we link this to our existing APM? We use NewRelic and DataDog.
[00:06:20] Jules Kim: Yes, we have connectors. For a two-way integration, you can add a custom field with the Redwood rootpath id into your APM spans so cross-system navigation lands you back into the Console.
[00:06:31] [00:06:35] Priya Das: Back to encryption — where are keys managed for Dedicated? We need KMS in our cloud account or HSM on-prem.
[00:06:42] Samir Patel: For Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS keys in AWS and GCP. For Private/on-prem we can integrate with HSM via PKCS#11. I'll share the security doc with the API for key wrapping.
[00:06:54] [00:06:58] Marta Ruiz: Ok, can you show a request playback where the model is different but we want to compare responses?
[00:07:02] Jules Kim: Sure — here's the playback modal. Pick original request, choose target model variant (canary or quantized), and toggle tokens logging. The playback runs in a sandbox and returns a side-by-side diff with token counts, latency, and a quality score if you provide a golden set.
[00:07:20] Liam O'Neill: That diff — is it stored? Is it searchable later?
[00:07:24] Jules Kim: You can persist it as an audit artifact or discard after review. Persisted diffs get an ID and are searchable by request id, model variant, and user tags.
[00:07:33] [00:07:37] Tom Baker: We heard about automatic fallback to compatible models when capacity is constrained. How are fallbacks prioritized and visible in traces?
[00:07:45] Jules Kim: The routing engine has a policy layer. In traces you'll see a route decision span with the policy name and target model. If a fallback happens, that's shown as a child span with a reason code (e.g., capacity_limit, failed_kv_cache). You can query by reason code.
[00:07:59] Marta Ruiz: If a fallback to a cheaper variant happens, we'd like an automatic rollback if output quality drops. Do you do quality-based rollbacks?
[00:08:07] Jules Kim: Yes. Redwood Optimize hooks into your eval suite. If quality metrics for a rollout fall below a threshold, we can automatically rollback traffic. The Console ties eval results to traces so you can see which cohorts experienced degradation.
[00:08:21] [00:08:25] Priya Das: Compliance: do you provide audit logs for who ran a playback and exported a trace? We need that for audits.
[00:08:30] Rina Alvarez: Every action in the Console is logged with user, IP, timestamp, and whether the artifact was exported. We can keep logs for the retention window you set, and we support long-term archival to your storage.
[00:08:42] [00:08:45] Marta Ruiz: Great. A tactical question: can you show queries for finding all requests that hit model_timeout within the last 24 hours and contain more than 500 tokens?
[00:08:55] Jules Kim: Yes, the search bar accepts boolean filters. Example: error.code:model_timeout AND token_count:>500 AND timestamp:[now-24h TO now]. That returns a list of traces; you can bulk export or attach to an incident.
[00:09:10] [00:09:12] Samir Patel: We're also going to show how to embed traces into Jira issues automatically with context.
[00:09:17] Jules Kim: Clicking the Integrations dropdown, you can configure an auto-create rule that posts the top trace and a link into Jira with a short summary and tags.
[00:09:28] Liam O'Neill: On cost: how much extra storage does retaining traces for 90 days add? We have cost sensitivity.
[00:09:36] Samir Patel: We can provide an estimate based on your sample rate and average trace size. For the pilot, we'll run a 24-hour synthetic and provide a projected monthly delta in the pricing sheet.
[00:09:48] [00:09:50] Marta Ruiz: Can we set sampling rules? For example, keep 100% of errors and 1% of success traces.
[00:09:56] Jules Kim: Absolutely. Sampling rules are policy-based: by status, by route, or by header. You can make exceptions for certain user ids or customers.
[00:10:07] [00:10:10] Tom Baker: Operational question — when an incident is ongoing, can SREs temporarily increase sampling for a specific service for 30 minutes?
[00:10:17] Jules Kim: Yes, there's a 'turbo' mode you can toggle from the incident view which increases sample rate and preserves all traces for a configurable window. It's auditable and can be restricted by RBAC.
[00:10:29] Marta Ruiz: Ok good. What do we need to kick off the pilot?
[00:10:33] Samir Patel: We'll need three things: network allowlist entries for our demo endpoint (if you're running Dedicated we'll provide IPs), a short whitelist of routes to preserve full traces for, and a point of contact for the first week of the pilot.
[00:10:45] [00:10:50] Liam O'Neill: I'll provide the IP allowlist and a set of real trace IDs we saw last month.
[00:10:55] Marta Ruiz: And Priya will want to review the KMS keywrap flow.
[00:10:59] Priya Das: Yes. Also, we need a signed DPA before sending any traces with real data.
[00:11:04] Samir Patel: Noted — I'll circulate the DPA and SOC2 package after the call.
[00:11:10] Jules Kim: Final demo note — the request timeline view supports annotations. If you annotate a span it becomes part of the audit trail, which is useful for handoffs between on-call and product.
[00:11:21] Tom Baker: Nice. One last technical point — our infra team uses a mixture of k8s and VM pools. Does Redwood's runtime need a specific container runtime?
[00:11:31] Jules Kim: The runtime is container-friendly; we provide Helm charts for k8s and systemd units for VMs. For Private installs we ship an operator that handles model artifact syncing, kernel selection, and healthchecks.
[00:11:44] Marta Ruiz: Perfect. Let's recap next steps.
[00:11:48] Samir Patel: Recap: Samir will send SOC2, DPA, network allowlist template, and pricing spreadsheet. Jules will stand up a demo tenant and a 24h synthetic run. Liam will give example traces and IPs. We'll schedule a follow-up call next week to kick off the pilot.
[00:12:04] Priya Das: We'll review KMS/HSM details and confirm whether Private is required or Dedicated suffices.
[00:12:10] Marta Ruiz: Thanks, everyone. That was helpful.
[00:12:13] Samir Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up with docs and parter links. Bye.

Notes about transcription: there are occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 1) and some model/flag names may be transcribed imperfectly. The Console UI elements mentioned (Trace Map, Request Playback, KV cache) are approximate labels used in the demo.
